entry.title: The all-night counter
entry.summary: A shop that never closes, or opens again at midnight: bar traffic, night shifts, students, and whoever else is out.

entry.title: The Polish bakery counter
entry.summary: A Polish-American bakery selling pączki — rich filled donuts, powidła or rose-petal jam inside, powdered or glazed — beside rye bread and coffee cake. One day a year it is the only thing anyone is there for.

entry.title: The Delta grocery counter
entry.summary: A small family grocery in the Mississippi or Arkansas Delta with a hot counter — and, in some of them, donuts fried in the morning beside the rest of the cooking.

entry.title: Dunkin' country
entry.summary: Coffee first, donut second, at a counter that measures itself in how fast the line moves. The New England model, and the one the rest of the country meets as a drive-thru.

entry.title: The malasada counter
entry.summary: A bakery counter in Hawaii selling malasadas — no hole, no filling by default, rolled in sugar — by the dozen in a box or hot by the piece in a bag.

entry.title: The beignet stand
entry.summary: An open-air or walk-up counter selling square fried dough under powdered sugar, three to an order, with coffee cut with chicory beside it.

entry.title: The orchard window
entry.summary: A seasonal counter at a cider mill, orchard or farm stand, running one machine and one product: cake donuts with cider in the batter, sugared and handed over hot in a paper bag.

entry.title: The Southwest burrito counter
entry.summary: A donut shop in New Mexico, Arizona or west Texas that also wraps breakfast burritos to order: scrambled egg, potato, cheese and chile in a flour tortilla, sold at the same window as the glazed.

entry.title: The novelty shop
entry.summary: A shop that competes on invention: unusual toppings, themed rooms, names that are jokes, and a queue that photographs its order.

entry.title: The New York corner counter
entry.summary: Donuts sold from a deli, bodega or coffee shop rather than a donut shop: a tray by the register, a grill behind the counter, and a bacon egg and cheese on a kaiser roll doing most of the business.

entry.title: Fastnacht Day in the Dutch counties
entry.summary: One pastry, one day. Potato-dough donuts, square or diamond cut, fried for Shrove Tuesday and eaten with butter or golden syrup, sold by bakeries, churches, fire halls and — in eastern Pennsylvania — most chain…

entry.title: The Southern California pink box
entry.summary: An independent counter, usually in a strip mall, usually open before five in the morning, frying both doughs in one small kitchen and selling them out of a matte pink box.

entry.title: The hot light
entry.summary: A glazed raised ring handed over hot, minutes out of the fryer, with the glaze still moving. Built around a window you can watch the line through, and a lit sign that says the fryer is running.

entry.title: The Texas kolache counter
entry.summary: A donut counter that also sells kolaches — and, in Texas, mostly klobasniky: sausage, ham, egg, cheese or jalapeño wrapped in sweet kolache dough.

entry.title: The mix-and-sign shop
entry.summary: An independently owned shop trading under a shared name and buying its dry mix from one supplier. It looks like a chain from the road and is not one at the till.

entry.title: Apple fritter
entry.summary: Chopped apple and cinnamon folded through raised dough, torn rather than cut, fried craggy and glazed all over so the sugar catches in every fold. No two come out the same shape.

entry.title: Bavarian cream
entry.summary: A raised round with no hole, filled with a set custard — Bavarian cream is custard lightened with whipped cream and held with gelatin — and finished in sugar, or iced with chocolate, at which point most counters call it…

entry.title: Bear claw
entry.summary: A sweet yeast dough — bread dough carrying more shortening than usual — filled with almond paste and sometimes raisins, shaped in a semicircle with slices cut along the curved edge so the sections separate as it proofs…

entry.title: Beignet
entry.summary: A deep-fried pastry of French origin, in New Orleans a square of dough fried until it puffs hollow and buried in confectioner's sugar. Beignet means bump.

entry.title: Bismarck
entry.summary: A round raised donut with no hole, fried, then injected with fruit preserve, custard or cream and finished in sugar or icing.

entry.title: Buttermilk bar
entry.summary: Cake batter cut in a bar rather than a ring, fried so it splits open along the top, and glazed heavily enough that the glaze runs into the split.

entry.title: Cake donut
entry.summary: A ring of thick batter, not dough, raised by baking powder or soda rather than yeast and dropped straight into the fat from a depositor.

entry.title: Chocolate cake
entry.summary: A cake ring with cocoa in the batter, glazed or sugared. Dark, dense, and sweeter than the plain cake ring on the published numbers.

entry.title: Cider donut
entry.summary: An American cake donut flavoured with apple cider, cinnamon and nutmeg in the batter, usually rolled in cinnamon or granulated sugar.

entry.title: Donut holes
entry.summary: The centres cut out of ring donuts, fried and sold by the bag — or, more often now, made on purpose from the same dough or batter and never cut from anything.

entry.title: Fastnacht
entry.summary: A Pennsylvania Dutch fried donut, often made with potato dough, eaten in the days of Carnival and above all on Shrove Tuesday.

entry.title: French cruller
entry.summary: A ring extruded from choux paste — flour cooked into butter and water, then beaten with eggs — piped through a star tip so it fries up ridged and hollow, and glazed thin. No yeast, no baking powder: steam lifts it.

entry.title: Glazed raised
entry.summary: A ring of yeast dough, proofed until it is full of gas, fried about two and a half minutes, then dragged through a thin sugar glaze while it is still hot enough to melt it. The glaze sets into a shell you can hear.

entry.title: Long John
entry.summary: A bar-shaped raised donut, glazed all over or iced on top, sometimes filled with custard or cream.

entry.title: Malasada
entry.summary: A flattened round of yeasted dough, fried and rolled in sugar — cinnamon sugar, often — with no hole and traditionally no filling.

entry.title: Maple bar
entry.summary: A bar of raised dough, fried, then topped end to end with maple-flavoured icing. Sometimes filled with custard or cream; sometimes finished with chopped bacon, which is a newer idea and an argued one.

entry.title: Mochi donut
entry.summary: A chewy donut made with glutinous rice flour or tapioca flour, usually formed as a ring of eight connected balls that pull apart. Moist, springy, and heavier in the hand than it looks.

entry.title: Old-fashioned
entry.summary: A cake ring with a cracked surface and tapered edges, glazed or sugared so the glaze pools in the cracks. The crack is the point: more surface, crisper edge, and a ring that holds up to coffee longer than a raised one.

entry.title: Pączki
entry.summary: A Polish filled donut: a flattened ball of rich dough — eggs, fat, sugar, yeast, sometimes milk — deep fried, filled with jam or cream, and finished in powdered sugar, icing, glaze or dried orange zest.

entry.title: Spudnut
entry.summary: A donut made with potato flour or mashed potato in the dough. Softer crumb, longer shelf life, and a faint savoury note under the sugar.

entry.title: Sufganiyah
entry.summary: A round filled donut, traditionally red jelly with icing sugar on top, eaten at Hanukkah. Dulce de leche fillings became common after South American immigration to Israel early in this century.

entry.title: Bacon, egg and cheese
entry.summary: Bacon, fried or scrambled egg and cheese on bread — in New York City, on a kaiser roll. About 20 grams of fat and 350 calories in a typical one.

entry.title: Biscuits and gravy
entry.summary: Soft wheat biscuits split and covered in a white gravy built on sausage drippings, flour and milk.

entry.title: Boba
entry.summary: Tea with milk and tapioca pearls, sealed under a film lid and drunk through a fat straw.

entry.title: Breakfast burrito
entry.summary: Breakfast inside a flour tortilla: scrambled egg, potato, cheese, and in the Southwest, New Mexico chile, jalapeño, salsa, onion, chorizo or bacon.

entry.title: Coffee with chicory
entry.summary: Coffee blended with roasted chicory root and cut half-and-half with hot milk.

entry.title: Egg roll
entry.summary: A cylindrical deep-fried roll in a thick wheat skin — shredded cabbage, chopped meat, sometimes shrimp — eaten with the fingers out of a cellophane packet of duck sauce.

entry.title: Fried rice and chow mein
entry.summary: Cooked rice stir-fried with egg, vegetables and meat, held hot in a steam table beside the donut case — with chow mein next to it in many shops.

entry.title: Klobasnek
entry.summary: Sausage — klobása, traditionally — wrapped in kolache dough and baked. Ham, egg, cheese, jalapeño and hot dog are all standard now, and in some Texas shops boudin, the Cajun pork-and-rice sausage.

entry.title: Kolache
entry.summary: A sweet bread with a well of fruit or cheese in the middle of puffy yeast dough — tvaroh, jam, poppy seed, or povidla, which is prune. Baked, not fried.

entry.title: The pot of coffee
entry.summary: Drip coffee from a glass pot on a warmer, in a paper cup or a mug, refilled by whoever is at the counter.

entry.title: The batter and the depositor
entry.summary: A thick chemically-leavened batter dropped straight into hot fat through a hand-held or bench depositor, which forms the ring as it falls.

entry.title: Day-old
entry.summary: Yesterday's donuts, sold cheap the next morning, usually bagged rather than boxed and usually the rings rather than the filled ones.

entry.title: The filler
entry.summary: A hand pump or bench machine that pushes jam, custard or cream through a nozzle into the side of a fried round.

entry.title: What is in the kettle
entry.summary: The fat itself: lard, beef tallow, vegetable shortening, or liquid oils — canola, soybean, palm.

entry.title: The glaze table
entry.summary: A shallow pan of thin sugar glaze beside the fryer, where raised rings are dragged through face-down within a minute of coming out of the fat.

entry.title: Cutting by hand
entry.summary: Rolling sheeted dough and cutting rings with a two-ring cutter, rather than depositing or buying pre-formed shells.

entry.title: The proof box
entry.summary: A warm humid cabinet where cut rings take their final rise before they go in the fat.

entry.title: Dipping and sprinkles
entry.summary: Icing in flat pans, sprinkles in bins: a donut is dipped face-down, then set in the sprinkles while the icing is still wet.

entry.title: The night shift
entry.summary: The hours the work actually happens in: dough started in the small hours so the case is full when the door opens.

entry.title: The case
entry.summary: The glass case: trays by kind, tongs on a hook, and a layout that repeats across the country without anyone having agreed on it.

entry.title: The kettle
entry.summary: A shallow open kettle of hot fat with a screen, where every donut in the shop is cooked, turned once, and lifted out.

entry.title: The raise
entry.summary: Baker's yeast fermenting a sweet dough until it is full of gas — once in bulk, once again after the rings are cut.

entry.title: Allie's Donuts
entry.summary: A shop on Route 2 in North Kingstown, Rhode Island, cutting its donuts by hand since 1968, and the state's landmark of the trade.

entry.title: Bob's Donuts and Pastries
entry.summary: A 24-hour counter on Polk Street in San Francisco, busiest after midnight, and two other locations.
